No.42

Seeking First, Then Letting Go — Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva on the Middle Way of Doing Good

Doing good may begin with wanting something, then slowly let go of clinging to reward.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I asked the Bodhisattva: people often say that doing good in hope of reward is impure, yet someone who feels nothing about good and evil and does nothing at all seems even worse. With what kind of heart should we do good for it to be right? Where is the line between goodness that seeks merit and goodness from a true heart?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

When first practicing goodness,
most have something they seek;
this is no great fault,
and better than not acting.
Doing good because of seeking,
the seed of goodness is already planted;
practicing long without turning back,
the heart gradually purifies itself.

If you seek fame and gain,
goodness easily runs out;
if you seek liberation,
goodness gradually becomes selfless.
Do not worry that your first intention
is not yet pure;
worry only that after long practice
you are unwilling to turn your heart.

Merit is not a sin;
clinging to merit becomes an obstacle.
To know that goodness can be cultivated,
to know that merit can be let go —
this is the Middle Way.
It is like a child
first learning to walk;
though encouraged by rewards,
in the end it stands on its own.

Goodness is the same:
from having something to gain,
it gradually comes to seeking nothing.
Seeking nothing is not cutting off,
but the fulfillment of compassion;
when the heart forgets the self,
good deeds flow on constantly.

🔶Plain Rendering

Most people who are just beginning to do good carry a wish to get something. This is no great fault — it is still better than not doing good at all. Doing good because you want something still plants the seed of goodness; as long as you keep at it for a long time without turning back, your heart will naturally become purer.

If what you seek is fame and gain, such goodness easily runs out one day; if what you seek is liberation, such goodness gradually becomes selfless.

Do not worry that your heart was not pure enough at the start; what you should really worry about is still being unwilling to change your mind after practicing for a long time.

Merit itself is not a fault; clinging to merit is what becomes an obstacle. Knowing that goodness must be cultivated, and also knowing that merit can be let go — this is the Middle Way.

It is just like a small child learning to walk: they may only take steps because of an adult's rewards and encouragement, but in the end they still learn to stand and walk on their own.

Doing good follows the same principle: from first seeking and gaining something, you slowly come to a state of seeking nothing.

And this "seeking nothing" is not giving up good deeds, but the natural fulfillment of compassion; when the heart has forgotten even the "me", good deeds keep flowing on naturally, like water.
